Distributed Energy Resources (DERs) often contribute low or temporary fault currents, complicating fault detection in active distribution systems.
Traditional overcurrent and distance protection schemes have intentional time delays for coordination, which can cause instability in DERs during faults.
Transient-based protection uses high-frequency current transients to quickly detect faults by comparing polarity at zone boundaries.
Rogowski coils are employed to measure high-frequency current transients due to their wide bandwidth and non-saturating characteristics.
The proposed hybrid scheme combines transient polarity comparison with conventional phasor-based protection for enhanced speed and security.
Only polarity information of the initial transient is exchanged between protection devices, requiring minimal communication bandwidth and no time synchronization.
The hybrid protection logic issues trip signals immediately upon confirmation of an internal fault without additional time delays.
Simulation studies were performed on a 230 kV transmission line feeding a 13.8 kV distribution system with a 3 MW synchronous generator.
The test system includes a microgrid capable of islanding, controlled by an intelligent electronic device at the point of interconnection.
The Rogowski coil output is processed through a high-pass filter with a 1 kHz cutoff frequency to extract transient components.
Communication delay between relays is assumed to be 10 ms, and circuit breaker operating time is assumed as 5 cycles.
The hybrid scheme reduces frequency and voltage deviations during faults, preserving DER stability.
The scheme is effective under weak infeed conditions caused by DERs, using permissive overreach transfer trip (POTT) distance protection.
Transient-based protection alone is vulnerable to false tripping due to non-fault transients, which is mitigated by supervision from conventional protection.
Simulation results demonstrate faster fault clearing times compared to conventional protection alone.
The equivalent circuit model of the Rogowski coil includes mutual inductance, coil self-inductance, resistance, and capacitance.
The hybrid scheme can detect and isolate faults under high fault resistance and varying fault inception angles.
The protection for busbar faults can be provided by applying the hybrid protection concept as a separate zone.
The proposed method was tested on the IEEE 34-bus feeder to demonstrate applicability to larger distribution networks.
The hybrid protection scheme improves overall protection coordination while maintaining security and speed.
